actions.result: Home readings over past 2 weeks: BP ranges 128-148/78-90 mmHg, resting pulse 62-96/min, irregular pulse noted on several mornings per patient log.

actions.result: No visible neck vein distension at 45 degrees; no ankle or pretibial edema seen on camera; no digital clubbing.

actions.name: Camera inspection of thyroid/neck
actions.result: No visible goiter or neck masses; no tremor of outstretched hands observed.

actions.name: Review 14-day patch monitor report
actions.result: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, AF burden 9%, longest episode 6 hours 40 minutes, ventricular rates during AF up to 148/min, sinus rhythm the remainder of the time; no sustained VT.

actions.name: Review transthoracic echocardiogram report
actions.result: Left atrium mildly dilated (volume index 32 mL/m2), left ventricular ejection fraction 55%, no significant valvular disease, no LV hypertrophy, no intracardiac thrombus visualized.

actions.name: Review renal function and electrolytes
actions.result: Sodium 139 mmol/L, Potassium 4.3 mmol/L, Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73m2 - all within normal limits.

actions.name: Review hemoglobin A1c
actions.result: Hemoglobin A1c 7.2% (goal <7.0-7.5% individualized) - mildly above target.

actions.name: Review liver function tests
actions.result: AST 24 U/L, ALT 28 U/L, both within normal limits.

actions.name: Calculate CHA2DS2-VASc score
actions.result: CHA2DS2-VASc = 2 (hypertension 1 point + diabetes 1 point + age 61 [0, below 65 threshold] + male sex [0 points]); estimated annual stroke risk approximately 2.2%.

actions.name: Administer STOP-BANG obstructive sleep apnea screening questionnaire
actions.result: Patient endorses loud snoring, witnessed apneas (per wife), daytime sleepiness, and hypertension on direct questioning; BMI 29.7 (not >35), age 61 (not >50 threshold not met for this component per standard cutoff... ) - components should be tallied from the interview; no validated composite score has been calculated or recorded in the chart.

actions.name: Review current medication list
actions.result: Losartan 50 mg daily, Metformin 1000 mg twice daily; no current anticoagulant or antiarrhythmic prescribed.

actions.name: Review in-office vitals from referring PCP visit
actions.result: BP 138/86 mmHg, HR 78/min irregular, weight 94 kg, height 178 cm, BMI 29.7.

actions.name: Review prior PCP referral note
actions.result: Referral note documents smartwatch alert for irregular rhythm, two months of palpitation episodes, and request for cardiology evaluation and anticoagulation discussion requested.

artifacts.title: 14-Day Ambulatory Patch Monitor Report
artifacts.author: Cardiac Monitoring Service
artifacts.body:
PATIENT: Samuel Adeyemi, 61M. Monitoring duration: 14 days 2 hours.

FINDINGS:
- Predominant rhythm: Sinus rhythm with normal AV conduction.
- Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation detected: total AF burden 9% of monitored time.
- Number of AF episodes: 11. Longest episode duration: 6 hours 40 minutes.
- Ventricular rate during AF: average 112/min, maximum 148/min.
- No sustained ventricular tachycardia. Rare isolated PVCs (<1% burden).
- No significant bradycardia or pauses >2.5 seconds.

IMPRESSION: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, burden 9%, with episodes of rapid ventricular response.

artifacts.title: Transthoracic Echocardiogram Report
artifacts.author: Echocardiography Lab
artifacts.body:
STUDY: Transthoracic echocardiogram, resting.

LEFT VENTRICLE: Normal size and wall thickness. Ejection fraction 55% (normal), estimated by biplane Simpson's method. No regional wall motion abnormality.

LEFT ATRIUM: Mildly dilated, volume index 32 mL/m2 (normal <34 mL/m2 borderline-mild dilation).

VALVES: Mild mitral annular calcification, no significant stenosis or regurgitation. Aortic and tricuspid valves structurally normal.

RIGHT HEART: Normal RV size and function. Estimated PA systolic pressure 28 mmHg (normal).

PERICARDIUM: No effusion.

INTRACARDIAC: No thrombus visualized (transthoracic study, limited sensitivity for LAA thrombus).

IMPRESSION: Mildly dilated left atrium. Preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (55%). No significant valvular disease.

facts.chart: Referred after smartwatch detected irregular rhythm; reports 2 months of intermittent chest fluttering and fatigue
facts.says: My smartwatch kept telling me my heart rhythm looked irregular, and I've been having these spells where my chest flutters and I feel wiped out afterward.

facts.chart: Episodes of palpitations occur roughly 2-3 times per week, lasting 1 to several hours, over the past 2 months
facts.says: It happens maybe two or three times a week. Sometimes it only lasts an hour, but a couple times it went on most of the afternoon.

facts.chart: Describes fatigue and mild breathlessness during episodes; denies chest pain or syncope
facts.says: During the episodes I feel tired, maybe a little short of breath, but no real pain and I've never passed out.

facts.chart: No clear identified trigger; occurs with activity and at rest, including after wine on weekends
facts.says: I can't really pin down what sets it off. Sometimes I'm just sitting at my desk, sometimes after a glass of wine on a Saturday.

facts.chart: Denies syncope; occasional mild lightheadedness during rapid episodes
facts.says: I've gotten a little dizzy once or twice when my heart was racing, but I never actually fainted.

facts.chart: Denies exertional chest pain or pressure; no anginal symptoms
facts.says: No chest pain, no pressure, nothing like that. Just the fluttering feeling.

facts.chart: Denies leg swelling or recent weight gain
facts.says: My ankles aren't swollen and my weight's been pretty steady.

facts.chart: Hypertension diagnosed approximately 8 years ago, on losartan 50 mg daily
facts.says: I've had high blood pressure for about eight years now, I take the losartan pill every morning.

facts.chart: Type 2 diabetes diagnosed approximately 5 years ago, on metformin, last A1c 7.2%
facts.says: I've got type 2 diabetes too, been about five years, I'm on the metformin twice a day.

facts.chart: No prior history of heart attack, heart failure, or stroke
facts.says: Never had a heart attack or anything like that before, no strokes either.

facts.chart: No known thyroid disease
facts.says: No thyroid problems that I know of.

facts.chart: Brother had an intracranial hemorrhage while on warfarin approximately 10 years ago
facts.says: My older brother had a brain bleed years back when he was on warfarin, that's actually one reason I'm really nervous about blood thinners.

facts.chart: Father had hypertension; no known family history of early coronary disease or sudden cardiac death
facts.says: My dad had high blood pressure too, but nobody in the family dropped dead young or anything like that.

facts.chart: Drinks 3-4 glasses of wine on weekend evenings, denies daily drinking
facts.says: I'll have maybe three or four glasses of wine on a Friday or Saturday night with my wife, nothing during the week though.

facts.chart: Wife reports loud snoring and witnessed pauses in breathing during sleep
facts.says: My wife says I snore like a freight train and sometimes she pokes me because it sounds like I stopped breathing.

facts.chart: Reports mild daytime fatigue and occasional dozing during afternoon meetings
facts.says: Honestly I've caught myself nodding off in a couple of afternoon work calls lately, which never used to happen.

facts.chart: Works as an accountant, currently in tax season with long hours
facts.says: It's tax season, so I'm putting in long hours at my desk, which honestly might be part of why I'm so tired.

facts.chart: Drinks 2-3 cups of coffee daily, no recent increase
facts.says: I drink my two or three cups of coffee a day, same as I always have.

facts.chart: Never smoker
facts.says: I've never smoked, not once in my life.

facts.chart: Denies recreational drug use or stimulant supplements
facts.says: No, nothing like that, I don't take any supplements or anything for energy.

facts.chart: Not currently on any anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication
facts.says: I'm not on any blood thinner right now, no.

facts.chart: Reports taking losartan every morning without missed doses
facts.says: I take that losartan every single morning without fail, I'm pretty disciplined about my pills.

facts.chart: Checks home BP and pulse most mornings using a validated wrist device; occasionally skips weekends
facts.says: I check my blood pressure most mornings with my wrist cuff, though I'll admit I sometimes skip it on weekends.

facts.chart: Expresses significant anxiety about anticoagulation given family history of hemorrhage, has researched alternatives online
facts.says: I've read a lot online about this, and honestly the idea of being on a blood thinner for the rest of my life scares me, especially after what happened to my brother.

facts.chart: Highly numerate, has researched AF ablation and left atrial appendage closure devices online
facts.says: I've looked into things like the ablation procedure and that little device that closes off part of the heart, I want to understand all my options before we decide anything.

facts.chart: Follows a moderately low-sodium diet per diabetes education, occasional fast food on work days
facts.says: I try to watch my salt because of my blood pressure, but during tax season I'll grab fast food more than I should.

facts.chart: Walks 30 minutes most days, denies exertional limitation outside of palpitation episodes
facts.says: I walk about half an hour most days, and other than when the fluttering hits I don't feel limited.

facts.chart: Denies orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
facts.says: I sleep fine on one pillow, no waking up gasping or anything.

facts.chart: Primary goals are to understand stroke risk, avoid long-term warfarin if possible, and explore whether rhythm control or procedures could reduce episodes
facts.says: What I really want to know is: how worried should I be about stroke, is there anything besides warfarin, and can we actually fix this rhythm problem instead of just living with it?

facts.chart: Reports high stress during tax season but denies this as sole cause of palpitations given objective monitor findings
facts.says: Work stress is through the roof right now, but I don't think stress alone explains the fluttering since the monitor actually caught something.

facts.chart: Denies erectile dysfunction symptoms
facts.says: No issues in that department, no.

facts.chart: Notes some palpitation episodes have occurred the morning after weekend wine consumption
facts.says: Now that you mention it, a couple of the worst flutter episodes were the morning after we'd had wine the night before.

objectives.text: Confirm and characterize paroxysmal atrial fibrillation using home monitor data, patch monitor report, and guided pulse self-examination.
Calculate stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc) and formulate an evidence-based anticoagulation recommendation despite patient reluctance rooted in family history.

Screen for and address reversible/contributing factors: obstructive sleep apnea, alcohol use ('holiday heart'), and thyroid dysfunction, by directly interviewing the patient about snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, and nocturnal symptoms.
Integrate echocardiogram findings (preserved EF, mildly dilated LA) into overall risk stratification and rule out structural causes requiring escalation.

Counsel the patient on anticoagulation options beyond warfarin (e.g., direct oral anticoagulants) and discuss rhythm-control strategies within cardiology scope, including when to refer for electrophysiology evaluation (ablation, left atrial appendage closure).

Identify the mismatch between patient's reported strict medication adherence and home monitoring data suggesting undertreated blood pressure variability, and between reported wine-only-on-weekends and the temporal link to palpitation episodes.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (9% burden on 14-day monitor, rates to 148/min) with preserved ejection fraction, in a patient with hypertension and diabetes (CHA2DS2-VASc 2), with possible contributing undiagnosed obstructive sleep apnea and alcohol-related triggering.
differential: Alcohol-triggered atrial fibrillation ('holiday heart' pattern) contributing to episodes
Obstructive sleep apnea as a possible reversible contributor/trigger to AF, warranting screening and sleep study referral
Thyrotoxicosis-related atrial fibrillation (excluded by normal TSH/T4)
Anxiety or stimulant-related palpitations (excluded given objective monitor-documented AF)
keyFindings: 14-day patch monitor: paroxysmal AF, 9% burden, longest episode 6h40m, max ventricular rate 148/min
Echocardiogram: EF 55%, mildly dilated LA, no valvular disease, no thrombus seen
TSH and renal/liver labs normal; A1c 7.2% (mildly above goal)

History of witnessed apneas/loud snoring per wife and reluctantly-disclosed daytime sleepiness raises suspicion for OSA, but no validated STOP-BANG score or objective oximetry data has been obtained in this case - formal sleep evaluation is needed
Several worst palpitation episodes occurred the morning after weekend wine intake
Home log shows intermittent irregular/elevated resting pulse and BP spikes despite reported perfect losartan adherence
plan: Discuss CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 and recommend oral anticoagulation per guidelines; explore patient's specific fears about warfarin and offer a direct oral anticoagulant (e.g., apixaban or rivaroxaban) as an alternative with lower intracranial hemorrhage risk; renal function (eGFR 82, creatinine 1.0) does not require dose reduction, noting that apixaban dose reduction criteria are based on age ≥80, weight ≤60kg, and creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL (none met) rather than eGFR alone, and rivaroxaban dosing is adjusted only at eGFR <50
Refer for formal in-lab or home polysomnography given reported snoring, witnessed apneas, and daytime sleepiness suggestive of OSA; treating OSA may reduce AF burden
Counsel on reducing/eliminating weekend alcohol intake given temporal association with episodes
Continue losartan for hypertension; coordinate with primary care on optimizing blood pressure control given variable home readings

Discuss rate vs rhythm control strategy; given symptomatic episodes and patient interest, consider referral to electrophysiology for discussion of catheter ablation; AF burden and LA size do not currently suggest urgent need for left atrial appendage closure device, which is typically reserved for anticoagulation-ineligible patients
Reinforce diabetes management; recommend primary care follow-up on A1c given mild elevation above individualized goal
No echocardiographic finding (preserved EF, no severe structural disease) requires escalation to heart failure or surgical referral at this time
Schedule follow-up after sleep study and initiation of anticoagulation to reassess symptoms and burden
redFlags: Any report of syncope, chest pain at rest, or signs of heart failure would warrant urgent escalation (not currently present)
Untreated OSA and continued alcohol use may increase AF burden and undermine rhythm control efforts
Declining anticoagulation entirely despite CHA2DS2-VASc 2 carries meaningful stroke risk (~2.2%/year) that must be clearly communicated
educationPoints: CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 in a male patient meets threshold for guideline-recommended anticoagulation regardless of AF burden percentage

Direct oral anticoagulants have significantly lower rates of intracranial hemorrhage compared to warfarin, which is important when counseling patients with a family history of warfarin-associated bleeding

DOAC dose-reduction criteria are drug-specific and based on age, weight, and creatinine (apixaban) or creatinine clearance (rivaroxaban) rather than eGFR alone; eGFR is used mainly to confirm adequate renal function and screen for contraindication

Obstructive sleep apnea is a major modifiable risk factor for atrial fibrillation recurrence and burden; screening (e.g., STOP-BANG) and treatment should be part of comprehensive AF management, though a formal diagnosis requires sleep study referral rather than interview alone
Alcohol, even in a weekend-only 'binge' pattern, can precipitate atrial fibrillation episodes ('holiday heart') and should be addressed in lifestyle counseling
Patient-reported medication adherence should be corroborated with objective home monitoring data when available, as perceived adherence does not always correlate with consistent physiologic control

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he takes losartan every single morning without ever missing a dose
mismatches.recordEvidence: Home BP/pulse trend log (d7) shows recurring days with systolic BP spikes to 140-148 mmHg and pulse surges to 88-96 bpm roughly every 4th day despite reported perfect adherence
mismatches.teachingPoint: Perceived adherence does not guarantee consistent pharmacodynamic control; cyclical BP/pulse spikes may reflect missed doses, timing issues, or AF episodes themselves rather than true medication failure, and warrant exploration rather than acceptance at face value.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient initially frames his wine drinking as weekend-only and separate from his symptoms, only later connecting worst episodes to the morning after drinking
mismatches.recordEvidence: 14-day patch monitor report (d1) documents 11 AF episodes with the longest lasting 6 hours 40 minutes, a pattern consistent with alcohol-triggered paroxysmal AF when cross-referenced with the home log's weekend timing
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may not spontaneously connect lifestyle triggers to objective arrhythmia data; direct, specific questioning about timing of alcohol intake relative to symptom onset can reveal clinically actionable triggers like alcohol-induced AF.

Review the available history, records, and guided exam findings; counsel him on diagnosis, stroke risk, and management options within cardiology's scope.

profile.title: New-Onset Paroxysmal Atrial Fibrillation Detected by Smartwatch in a 61-Year-Old with Hypertension and Diabetes
profile.summary: A 61-year-old accountant with hypertension and type 2 diabetes is referred to cardiology after his smartwatch flagged an irregular rhythm, confirmed as paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (9% burden) on a 14-day patch monitor with preserved ejection fraction on echocardiogram. The case teaches CHA2DS2-VASc-based anticoagulation decision-making in a patient fearful of 'blood thinners' due to a family bleeding history, while screening for reversible contributors (obstructive sleep apnea, alcohol) and reconciling a patient-reported adherence versus home-monitoring mismatch.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home office in New Jersey
